description_ru: Вымышленная новость о шестимесячном эксперименте в городе Бриндлмур: торговцы, жители и водители спорят о закрытии центра для машин.
text:
BRINDLEMOOR - The medieval heart of Brindlemoor fell unusually quiet on Monday morning, as a six-month experiment banning private cars from the city centre began under grey skies and a certain amount of public scepticism.

Concrete planters, bollards and a team of stewards in yellow jackets now guard the seven streets inside the old walls, where residents, delivery vans, buses and bicycles still have access but ordinary traffic does not. The council, which approved the scheme after two years of consultation, describes it as a "living laboratory", a phrase that has already acquired a mildly ironic ring among shopkeepers.

"We are not trying to punish anyone," said Councillor Aurelio Banks, who chairs the transport committee. "We are trying to find out whether a town centre can work better when it is designed for people on foot. The only way to know is to try it, measure the results honestly and be willing to change our minds." Sensors have been fitted to lamp posts to count pedestrians, monitor air quality and measure noise, and the data will be published every month.

The reasons for the trial are not hard to find. The narrow medieval streets, built for carts and not for cars, have long been clogged at peak times, and the council's figures suggest that the centre exceeded legal limits for nitrogen dioxide on more than eighty days last year. A recent survey found that more than half of residents considered the area unpleasant to walk through, and a cyclist was seriously injured in a collision on Saddlers Lane in March, an incident that campaigners say hastened the decision.

Yet the plan has divided the town. Traders in the Cornmarket, a cobbled square lined with independent shops, fear that customers will simply go elsewhere. "People do not drive into town for pleasure," said Philippa Garrow, who has sold hats and gloves there for twenty-six years. "They come in the car, buy something heavy, put it in the boot and go home. If you take away the car, you take away the customer. I am afraid that the council has been listening to people who do not run businesses."

A similar anxiety was voiced by disabled residents, some of whom said that the exemptions system, which allows blue-badge holders to enter the zone, remained confusing and bureaucratic. "I am sure that the council means well," said Reuben Okoye, a retired teacher who uses a wheelchair, "but on the first morning I was stopped twice by stewards who did not know the rules. If this is to work, it has to work for everyone, and that includes people like me who cannot simply hop on a bicycle."

Supporters of the scheme point to the experience of other cities. In several European towns that have restricted traffic, early declines in takings were followed by modest increases, as pedestrians lingered longer and spent more on cafes and services. Dr Hannah Veldkamp, a transport researcher who has advised the council, cautioned that the transition could be rough. "The first three months are always the hardest," she said. "Habits are sticky. Shopkeepers see the empty road and panic before they see the extra footfall. But the evidence, though not universal, suggests that people who walk or cycle visit more often, even if they spend less each time."

On Monday itself the picture was mixed. Footfall in the central streets was down about twelve per cent compared with the same day last year, according to the council's preliminary count, though the cafes on Abbey Street reported a busy lunchtime. A group of schoolchildren played a noisy game of chase across the usually congested crossing at Market Cross, watched with amusement by a busker who confessed that he could finally hear his own guitar. "It is nicer, there is no doubt about it," he said. "Whether it is nicer for business, I leave to cleverer people than me."

The scheme has also encountered some unexpected side effects. Residents in the streets just beyond the walls say that traffic that used to pass through the centre is now spilling into their neighbourhoods. A handful of them gathered outside the town hall at lunchtime to hand in a petition with nearly four hundred signatures. "We were told that traffic would evaporate," said Imogen Prowse, who lives on Tanners Row. "It has not evaporated; it has moved house, and it has moved to mine." Councillor Banks promised that the committee would examine the problem within a fortnight and, if necessary, introduce a one-way system.

The final verdict, in any case, will come in September, when councillors will vote on whether to extend the ban, modify it or scrap it altogether. A public meeting has been scheduled for next month, and the council says it will publish a full evaluation, including the results of an independent economic study of retail takings in the zone.

For now, the town is watching itself with the nervous curiosity of a patient trying out a new treatment. By mid-afternoon on Monday, a queue of cyclists had formed outside the Cornmarket and a small group of shoppers were walking slowly down the middle of the street, looking up, perhaps for the first time in years, at the carved gables above the shops.

"I never noticed that clock," one of them said, pointing. "How long has it been there?" Since 1612, replied a passer-by, who had to speak up over the sound of birds.

questions.question: What is being tested in Brindlemoor?
questions.answer: A six-month ban on private cars in the city centre.

questions.question: Why does the hat seller oppose the plan?
questions.answer: She believes customers who come by car will go elsewhere.

questions.question: What unexpected problem did residents outside the walls report?
questions.answer: Traffic is spilling into their neighbourhoods.

questions.question: When will councillors make a final decision?
